Renal and Genitourinary Disorders

Acute Kidney Injury

AKI in the ED is a time-sensitive physiology problem: identify prerenal, intrinsic, or postrenal injury, stabilize metabolic threats, stop ongoing nephron injury, and decide who needs observation, admission, nephrology, urology, or dialysis.

Board trap: A “small” creatinine rise can hide large nephron loss when baseline creatinine is low or renal function is changing fast.

ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

AKI is deterioration of renal function over hours to days with waste accumulation and loss of homeostasis. ED definitions based on creatinine, GFR, and urine output are helpful but imperfect because they assume steady state. Most community-acquired AKI is reversible if volume depletion, medication effect, infection, or obstruction is corrected early.

Tintinalli source

Table 88-1

AKIN and RIFLE criteria for acute kidney injury.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Renal function depends on filtration, reabsorption, secretion, renal blood flow, and autoregulation. AKI is classified as prerenal from decreased perfusion, intrinsic from renal parenchymal injury, and postrenal from obstruction. For many AKI causes, decreased renal blood flow is the final common pathway. Ischemic tubular necrosis adds inflammation, vasoconstriction, endothelial injury, tubular obstruction, and backleak.

Tintinalli source

Figure 88-1

Ischemic tubular necrosis mechanisms.

CLINICAL FEATURES

HISTORY AND COMORBIDITIES

AKI itself may be silent until uremia produces nausea, vomiting, drowsiness, fatigue, confusion, coma, or bleeding tendency. Search for volume loss, sepsis, heart failure, liver failure, burns, hemorrhage, medications, contrast, nephrolithiasis, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, glomerulonephritis symptoms, vasculitis, Goodpasture/Wegener clues, prostatic disease, catheter problems, and malignancy.

Anuria strongly suggests obstruction, but vascular catastrophe or fulminant intrinsic renal disease can also do it. Alternating oliguria and polyuria is highly suggestive of obstruction.

Tintinalli source

Table 88-2

Risk factors for acute kidney injury.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION

Assess volume status with mucous membranes, JVP, lung exam, edema, tissue turgor, weight change, and perfusion. Look for rash/vasculitis, jaundice, abdominal or pelvic mass, distended bladder, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, abdominal aortic aneurysm, abnormal pulses, pleural effusion, and pulmonary edema.

DIAGNOSIS

The ED goals are to recognize AKI risk, correct metabolic effects, prevent iatrogenic worsening, and sort prerenal/postrenal/intrinsic causes. Labs include CBC, electrolytes with magnesium/phosphorus, hepatic tests, urinalysis, urine indices/culture when indicated, cultures when infection is possible, ECG for hyperkalemia, chest radiography for volume/pneumonia, and bladder/renal ultrasound when obstruction is plausible.

PRERENAL ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY

Prerenal AKI follows hypovolemia, hypotension, low effective arterial volume, renal artery disease, or medications that reduce renal blood flow. It can progress to intrinsic ischemic injury if perfusion is not restored. The question is not just “dry or wet”; it is whether effective renal perfusion is adequate.

Tintinalli source

Table 88-3

Causes of prerenal acute kidney injury.

POSTRENAL ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY

Postrenal AKI is common in older adults and patients with prostate disease, catheters, GU surgery, stones, malignancy, retroperitoneal disease, or sphincter-affecting drugs. Bladder scan and renal ultrasound are high-yield; urethral catheter relieves lower obstruction, while ureteral obstruction may need urology.

INTRINSIC ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY

Intrinsic AKI injures glomerulus, tubule, interstitium, or vasculature. In community disease, drugs, infection, and vascular events are common; in hospital disease, ischemic and toxic insults dominate.

CONTRAST-INDUCED NEPHROPATHY

Contrast-associated creatinine changes are defined by creatinine rise after exposure, but modern data show confounding and selection bias. Hydration is still considered for CKD and high-risk patients when contrast is necessary, while life-threatening diagnoses can outweigh renal risk.

CRYSTAL-INDUCED NEPHROPATHY

Crystals precipitate within tubules and injure epithelium. Tumor lysis, acyclovir, sulfonamides, indinavir, triamterene, hypovolemia, CKD, and urinary pH matter.

ANGIOTENSIN-CONVERTING ENZYME INHIBITORS

ACE inhibitors and ARBs preferentially dilate the efferent arteriole, lowering GFR. They can precipitate significant AKI in bilateral renal artery stenosis, volume depletion, or combined vasoconstrictor use, and may cause hyperkalemia.

NSAIDS

NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated renal blood flow and GFR; chronic use can cause interstitial nephritis. Risk rises with age, CKD, heart failure, diabetes, volume depletion, diuretics, or ACE inhibitor/ARB use.

ANTIBIOTICS

Aminoglycosides, vancomycin, TMP-SMX, cephalosporins, fluoroquinolones, acyclovir, and valacyclovir are common renal offenders. Medication reconciliation is treatment, not paperwork, in AKI.

PIGMENT NEPHROPATHY

Hemoglobin or myoglobin from hemolysis or rhabdomyolysis obstructs and injures tubules. Heme-positive urine with few/no RBCs suggests myoglobinuria.

GLOMERULONEPHRITIS

Glomerulonephritis may be postinfectious, toxic, lupus/immune, Goodpasture, or vasculitic. Think of nephritic urine with hematuria, red cell casts, hypertension, decreased output, or nephrotic edema/proteinuria/hypoalbuminemia.

Table 88-4

Intrinsic acute kidney injury due to drugs.

DIAGNOSTIC TESTING

CREATININE AND GFR

Creatinine is useful but delayed and muscle-mass dependent. In no renal function it rises about 1 to 3 mg/dL per day; faster rise suggests rhabdomyolysis. Automated eGFR equations are unreliable in changing AKI because they assume steady state.

CYSTATIN C

Cystatin C is less affected by diet, drugs, and body mass, and may predict death or progression, but it also rises only after AKI has already occurred. It is not the missing early ED biomarker.

URINE OUTPUT

Urine output criteria require catheterized measurement over time, limiting ED usefulness. Still, oliguria/anuria is clinically important and should trigger obstruction and perfusion assessment.

BUN-TO-CREATININE RATIO

BUN-to-creatinine may suggest hypovolemia but is altered by GI bleeding, trauma, protein load, malnutrition, hepatic dysfunction, and poor performance in predicting fluid responsiveness.

FRACTIONAL EXCRETION OF SODIUM

FeNa can support prerenal versus tubular injury patterns but is confounded by diuretics, glomerulonephritis with volume depletion, and retained tubular concentrating capacity.

URINALYSIS

Urinalysis gives pattern recognition: hyaline casts can be prerenal, granular casts suggest tubular injury, red cell casts/proteinuria suggest glomerulonephritis, and heme-positive dip with no RBCs suggests myoglobinuria. Do not interpret urine indices without the clinical context.

IMAGING

Renal ultrasound detects hydronephrosis and can estimate chronicity by kidney size and echogenicity. Color Doppler can assess renal perfusion. CT can localize obstruction when ultrasound shows hydronephrosis or when stone/retroperitoneal disease is likely.

Tintinalli source

Figure 88-2

Normal kidney ultrasound compared with hydronephrosis.

TREATMENT

For critically ill AKI, resuscitation comes first while diagnostics run: treat hypovolemia, sepsis, myocardial ischemia, respiratory failure, heart failure, electrolyte disturbance, acidosis, volume overload, and obstruction. The underlying cause is the main treatment target.

VOLUME DEPLETION

Correct intravascular deficits with crystalloids. Balanced crystalloids may reduce adverse kidney outcomes compared with normal saline in some settings. Use bedside ultrasound and the overall exam to avoid fluid overload.

Tintinalli source

Figure 88-3

Inferior vena cava ultrasound for volume assessment.

PREVENTING RENAL INJURY

Hold nephrotoxins, adjust renal dosing, and weigh contrast risk against diagnostic benefit. Avoid gadolinium when GFR is very low. If contrast imaging is needed in abnormal renal function, hydrate based on comorbidities and urgency.

RELIEVE URINE OUTFLOW OBSTRUCTION

Relief of obstruction is time-sensitive; permanent loss may occur after 10 to 14 days of complete obstruction, and infection worsens risk. Consider urethral, ureteral, and sphincter causes.

FLUID OVERLOAD

Diuretics treat overload but do not prevent AKI in euvolemic patients. Failure to respond to diuretics may be a dialysis indication. The furosemide stress test can predict worsening AKI in selected mild cases.

HYPERTENSION

Fenoldopam and nicardipine are commonly used when severe hypertension contributes to AKI; choose agents based on end-organ threat and comorbidities.

METABOLIC ACIDOSIS

When pH is above 7.1, treat the AKI cause. With pH <=7.1, dialysis is preferred in anuria or fluid overload because bicarbonate requires urine flow and volume tolerance.

ELECTROLYTE DISORDERS

Hyperkalemia with ECG changes or confirmed significant elevation requires immediate stabilization and potassium-shifting/removal therapy. ECG sensitivity is imperfect, so proven severe hyperkalemia still matters.

GLOMERULONEPHRITIS TREATMENT

Management requires nephrology, biopsy planning, corticosteroids, cyclophosphamide when indicated, and consideration of plasmapheresis for selected rapidly progressive syndromes.

DISPOSITION AND CONSULTATION

Mild reversible prerenal AKI may fit ED observation. Failure to improve, severe AKI, uncertain etiology, obstruction requiring intervention, dangerous electrolytes, uremic symptoms, or intrinsic renal disease requires admission and often nephrology/urology consultation.

DIALYSIS/RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY

Timing is debated, but emergent dialysis is not. Use the dangerous indications: uncontrolled hyperkalemia, refractory overload/hypoxia, uremic pericarditis, progressive uremic encephalopathy/seizure, severe dysnatremia, severe metabolic acidosis with AKI, dialyzable life-threatening poisoning, uremic bleeding, or excessive azotemia judged in context. Dialysis is triggered by physiology, not a single creatinine number.

Table 88-7

Indications for emergent dialysis or renal replacement therapy.

SPECIAL POPULATIONS

CARDIORENAL SYNDROME

Cardiorenal syndrome links acute or chronic heart dysfunction with kidney dysfunction. Type 1 is acute cardiac deterioration causing AKI; type 3 is AKI causing cardiac injury or dysfunction; type 5 is systemic illness such as sepsis affecting both. Compare baseline creatinine and BNP to help identify primary driver. Treat acute heart failure while monitoring renal response; ultrafiltration is reserved for diuretic-refractory overload or life-threatening hyperkalemia/pulmonary edema.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen adds the acute heart-failure/cardiorenal mechanism and diuretic-resistance frame; Tintinalli remains the Ch88 AKI spine and supplies every Ch88 table/figure.

IV CONTRAST IN PATIENTS TAKING METFORMIN

Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is rare but feared in renal dysfunction. FDA guidance is conservative for eGFR 30 to 60 around iodinated contrast; ACR permits continuation when eGFR is >=30 and recommends holding at eGFR <=30 or AKI, then reassessing renal function after 48 hours. Follow local policy and the patient’s actual renal trajectory.
